extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, storytellers, and filmmakers studying story design
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for designing cinematic stories: Controlling Idea types, protagonist construction, levels of conflict, climax/irony, and the audience bond. Geared to writers crafting feature films and long-form dramatic narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Study your Story Climax and extract from it your Controlling Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every coherent tale expresses an idea veiled inside an emotional spell. Once you discover your Controlling Idea, respect it. Ask yourself: 'Is this the truth? Do I believe in the meaning of my story?' If the answer is no, toss it and start again. If yes, do everything possible to get your work into the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Controlling Ideas — Optimistic (Up-ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'up-ending' story: Goodness or the positive value triumphs (e.g., 'Goodness triumphs when we outwit evil').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include films where characters cast off illusions, listen to their hearts, and find love. Historically, an up-ending could be defined as 'The protagonist gets what he wants.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Controlling Ideas — Pessimistic (Down-ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'down-ending' story: expresses cynicism, loss, misfortune — a negatively charged vision in which the Counter-Idea prevails (e.g., 'The power of nature will have the final say over mankind’s futile efforts').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'down-ending' films show that nature or human evil prevails; they are rarer because the pessimistic vision is a hard truth some wish to avoid. Examples: THE BIRDS, THE ELEPHANT MAN, SCOTT OF THE ANTARCTIC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Controlling Ideas — Ironic (Up/Down-ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ironic Controlling Ideas merge optimism and pessimism: the story says both positive and negative truths simultaneously (e.g., 'Love is both pleasure and pain').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ironic climaxes express a dual charge: what is gained and what is lost, side by side. Irony differs from ambiguity (clarity is required) and from coincidence (must be honestly motivated). Irony is difficult to write and demands wisdom and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redemption Plot (positive irony pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A protagonist compulsively pursues contemporary values (success, fame, etc.) that will destroy them, but if they see the truth in time and throw away the obsession, they can redeem themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At climax the protagonist sacrifices his dream (positive), a value that has become a soul-corrupting fixation (negative), to gain an honest, sane, balanced life (positive). Examples: KRAMER VS. KRAMER, OUT OF AFRICA, TERMS OF ENDEARMENT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punitive Plot (negative irony pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a protagonist clings to obsession, they achieve their desire which then destroys them — the Counter-Idea becomes the Controlling Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Story Climax the protagonist achieves their desire (positive) only to be destroyed by it (negative). Examples: WALL STREET, CASINO, THE WAR OF THE ROSES.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony must be honest, clear, and non-coincidental
rubrics_metrics.description: A true irony is honestly motivated and clearly declares both positive and negative statements; it is not ambiguity or mere coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity blurs; irony is a clear, double declaration. Stories that end by random chance, even if doubly charged, are meaningless, not ironic. The two charges at climax must remain separated in the audience experience and not cancel each other out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as social influence — obligation to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists' primary responsibility is not to cure society but to tell the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given story’s persuasive power, ask whether the Controlling Idea is the truth you believe. If it is, publish; if not, discard. While stories can convey repellent ideas, censorship should be opposed; the marketplace of ideas must allow expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist is a willful character
rubrics_metrics.description: A PROTAGONIST is a willful character: the protagonist's will is the central driving force of story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality of will matters as much as quantity. Even seemingly passive protagonists must possess inner will that sustains desire through conflict and leads to irreversible change. A truly passive protagonist who wants nothing cannot carry a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist has a conscious desire
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist has a known, conscious desire — an object of desire they would be able to state if asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desire may be external (e.g., destroy the shark) or internal (e.g., maturity). A simple, clear conscious desire is often sufficient to drive the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist may have a self-contradictory unconscious desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorable protagonists often have both a conscious desire and an unconscious desire that contradict each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inner contradiction (what the character thinks he wants vs. what he actually wants unconsciously) adds complexity and audience interest; the unconscious desire should be perceivable by the audience even if the character is unaware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must have capacities to pursue desire convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's characterization must be believable and have the right combination of qualities to pursue the object of desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the protagonist fails, their desires must be realistic relative to will and capacities so the audience believes they could achieve the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must have at least a chance to attain desire
rubrics_metrics.description: An audience will not accept a protagonist who lacks any realistic possibility of fulfilling their wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hope (however hypothetical) is required. The protagonist must not be literally hopeless; the audience expects a minimum plausible chance of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must pursue desire to the human limit (the end of the line)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist must have the will and capacity to pursue their desire to the 'human limit' established by setting and genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story should swing to extremes and take the protagonist to absolute, irreversible change. Each story must find closure for itself even if sequels are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: A story must build to a final action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another
rubrics_metrics.description: The ending must answer the story's questions and reach closure so audience members don't exit imagining crucial scenes omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If viewers leave thinking 'shouldn’t she have done X before/after?', the ending is unsatisfying. Writers must take the audience to the limit where all questions are answered and emotions satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must be empathetic (not necessarily sympathetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PROTAGONIST must be empathetic — the audience must recognize something 'like me' in them; sympathy (likability) is optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empathy is the glue of audience involvement: it creates a vicarious rooting for the protagonist. Even unlikeable characters can be made empathetic by revealing shared human qualities (e.g., Macbeth's conscience). Without empathy, the audience/story bond breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: The audience bond is held by empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional involvement depends on the audience identifying with the protagonist; empathy makes the audience root for the character as if for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empathy is absolute; sympathy is optional. The writer's task is to create an empathetic center in the protagonist so the audience is invested in the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Step / Minimal Conservative Action
rubrics_metrics.description: At any moment characters take the minimum, conservative action from their point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human nature is conservative: characters will not expend more energy or risk than necessary. This subjective minimality should determine their actions; what seems extreme objectively will feel conservative to the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: In story the character's minimal action must provoke antagonism (the world's reaction differs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand difference between story and life: in story a character takes an action expecting a useful reaction, but instead the world's reaction provokes antagonism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers must craft moments where an apparently minimal action leads to forces of antagonism reacting differently or more powerfully than expected — this is where life becomes interesting in story. 'BUT NEVER, EVER IN A STORY' should the character get the expected enabling reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: World of a character — three levels of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's world consists of concentric circles of conflict: (1) the inner self (mind, body, emotion), (2) personal relationships (intimacy beyond social role), and (3) extra-personal conflict (social institutions, other individuals, environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story is born where subjective and objective realms touch; the protagonist's actions should encounter antagonism on one or more of these levels to generate dramatic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs with multiple protagonists — Plural vs Multiprotagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Plural-Protagonist: two or more characters share the same desire and mutually suffer/benefit. Multiprotagonist: multiple characters pursue separate desires and create multi-plot stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a Plural-Protagonist, conditions must be met: all individuals share the same desire; in pursuit they mutually suffer and benefit. Multiprotagonist stories weave smaller stories (each with its own protagonist) into a portrait of society (examples: NASHVILLE, PULP FICTION).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist need not be human
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist can be an animal, a cartoon, or even an inanimate object provided it can be given free will and desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anything capable of desire, action, and suffering consequences can function as a protagonist (examples: BABE, BUGS BUNNY, The Little Engine That Could).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Gap — where story is born
rubrics_metrics.description: STORY is born in the place where the subjective and objective realms touch: the protagonist seeks an object of desire beyond reach and takes an action he believes will help, but the objective realm reacts differently or more powerfully than expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'gap' between expected enabling reaction and actual antagonistic reaction creates drama. Plot scenes should exploit this gap for interest and conflict.
